item.title: As China Pushes to Expand in Asia, Trump Focuses on Iran
item.description:
It was the worst clash in years between China and the Philippines at a long-simmering flashpoint in the South China Sea.

For decades, the Philippines has claimed a small reef in disputed waters and signaled its control of the territory by rotating troops to a World War II-era ship grounded there. An international tribunal ruling a decade ago supports the Philippines’ claim.

But last month, a Chinese Coast Guard vessel began circling the ship, which is named the Sierra Madre. It was the latest in a long series of encounters between the two governments at the site, which is called the Second Thomas Shoal.

At one point, the Chinese Coast Guard used small boats to move in on Filipino service members and beat one of the men with a wooden baton, inflicting head injuries, according to Philippine and U.S. officials. China blamed the Philippines for provoking the clash.

The American ambassador expressed outrage and declared that the United States stood with the Philippines, the oldest U.S. treaty ally in Southeast Asia.

Yet no one expects China to curb its expansionist activities in the region anytime soon. And there are growing doubts among Asian nations over what the United States would be willing to do to deter China, given the enormous distraction and resource drain of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.

The United States is running low on critical weapons, including air defense interceptors. Iran’s missile and drone attacks have forced U.S. troops to leave bases in the Middle East and destroyed the sites, an indication of what the Chinese military — which is much more powerful than Iran’s — could do in a conflict in Asia.

In early July, China conducted a rare test firing of a nuclear-capable intercontinental ballistic missile that carried a dummy warhead, sending it into the Pacific Ocean from a nuclear-powered submarine. It is one of the most powerful elements in its arsenal.

While China tests its might, President Trump’s State Department is closing consulates in Japan and Indonesia, according to congressional officials briefed on the decision.

Mr. Trump’s second term “has been a colossal failure for U.S. interests in the Asia region,” Representative Gregory W. Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said in a statement.

“This strategy, if you can call it one, is a gift to China that is undermining U.S. credibility and harming our national security,” he added.

Trump appointees say the administration is not ceding ground in Asia. In a speech in Manila on Aug. 10, Elbridge Colby, the under secretary of defense for policy, said the Trump administration aimed to “maintain a posture of deterrence by denial along the first island chain” — meaning it was willing to commit military resources to dissuade China from invading or attacking islands that include Taiwan and ones in the Philippines and Japan.

But Mr. Colby also said allies needed to spend more on defense and should try to integrate their militaries with that of the United States — and “not vainly and futilely seek to exclude or supplant us.”

Mr. Trump’s global trade war, whose targets have included Southeast Asian nations, has also revealed to allies and partners that the United States can be a commercial antagonist.

The U.S. government has lacked an economic vision for Southeast Asia for years, as Democratic and Republican politicians retreated from a Pacific Rim trade pact that President Barack Obama promoted.

That has left countries in Southeast Asia wondering what happened to the U.S. drive to ensure that it remains a presence that balances against China.

While Southeast Asian countries do not want to be trapped in a great-power clash between the United States and China, “they still want to feel the United States is a healthy counterweight to the P.R.C.,” said Mira Rapp-Hooper, who served on the National Security Council during the Biden administration and is now a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution. She was using the initials for the formal name for China, the People’s Republic of China.

“So the perception that the United States is drifting as an alternative has also left a real impression on many of these partners,” she added.

While Mr. Trump has talked about China as an economic rival, he also embraced the superpower after it successfully retaliated during his tariff war last year.

During a summit in Beijing in May, Mr. Trump expressed admiration for President Xi Jinping of China, and he is preparing to host Mr. Xi at a state visit in Washington in late September.

Mr. Trump’s move to build what he calls a “G2” — Group of Two — relationship with China has upended a growing bipartisan push in Washington in the last decade to confront China as a hostile rival.

As the Trump-Xi bonhomie grows, some Asian countries are feeling left out, yet are also opting to stay on China’s friendly side.

That is especially true when China remains the largest trading partner for many of the countries, and the United States is not working on presenting economic alternatives.

“We’re in a very difficult position because you know we want to have that maximal relationship with both sides,” said Richard Heydarian, a political scientist from the Philippines. “And then for countries like the Philippines, it’s even more impossible because the U.S. is a military ally. We need the U.S. when it comes to the China threat, but the U.S. is not giving us much love on anything beyond the military aspect.”

The Biden administration agreed to work with the Philippines on expanding a transportation network, called the Luzon Economic Corridor, to better integrate the country into global supply chains.

The Trump administration is trying to bring the Philippines into its so-called Pax Silica initiative, with the notion of having the country work on semiconductor manufacturing and building artificial intelligence in a way that would benefit the United States.

But those nascent steps pale next to U.S. efforts to keep up its military ties with the Philippines. The two counties have long had a close relationship, and they have tried to maintain military cooperation, though their ties have shifted at times.

The United State made the Philippines its first colonial foothold in Asia after taking it from Spain in the Spanish-American War. And the Philippines is the only Southeast Asian nation that has a formal alliance treaty with the United States — one that requires their militaries to help with the defense of the other nation.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters in Manila last month during an annual forum of Southeast Asian nations that the U.S. military was determined to push back against China’s expansionist efforts.

“We’re never going to accept that international waterways are somehow under the control of other countries,” he said. “We’ll continue to sail through international waterways and freedom of navigation efforts of that kind, and we’ll continue to live up to our commitments — for example, with the Philippines and other countries — in terms of the treaty commitments that we have.”

During the Biden administration, the U.S. government took a hands-on approach to forging partnerships in Asia. It brought Japan into a security coalition with the Philippines. And President Joseph R. Biden Jr. got the Philippines to grant American troops expanded access to nine bases on islands near Taiwan.

In November 2022, Vice President Kamala Harris flew to the island of Palawan, east of the South China Sea, and visited a Philippine Coast Guard site there to send a signal to China.

The military cooperation has continued under Mr. Trump, despite the resource drain of the Iran war. In May, the U.S. and Philippine militaries tested a Typhon missile launcher at one of the islands, a public show with a weapon that could be deployed against Chinese troops if they tried to invade Taiwan.

The Philippines invited Japan to take part in multination military exercises in June, the first time since World War II that Japanese troops had been active on Philippine soil.

The move is both a continuation of the coalition overseen by the Biden administration and a hedge by the Philippines to broaden its partnerships beyond the United States.

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: Iran Says Qatar Captured Three of Its Pilots Early in War With U.S.
item.description:
Iran has accused Qatar of capturing three of its bomber pilots in the early days of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, and on Saturday called on the International Committee of the Red Cross to intervene on their behalf.

Gen. Seyed Mohammad Bagherzadeh, commander of the Iranian armed forces’ missing persons search committee, wrote to the global aid organization in a letter published by Iranian media. He said the men were flying Su-24 fighter jets in an operation on March 2, days after the outbreak of the war, when their planes had been hit by “enemy defenses” and the pilots ejected.

They survived but were captured by the Qatari authorities, according to General Bagherzadeh, who named the men as Javad Salehi, Abdolmajid Dashtian and Omran Behraveshian. A fourth pilot, Majid Kazemi, died, he added.

The Red Cross and a Qatari government spokesman did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

General Bagherzadeh’s letter was the most precise indication so far of what Iran believes happened to the three pilots. Before Saturday’s letter, Iranian authorities had said the fate of the men was unknown.

Qatar, a close U.S. ally that hosts a major American military base, said on March 2 that its Air Force had shot down two Iranian Su-24 bomber jets. Iran lashed out at its Persian Gulf neighbors soon after it was attacked by the United States and Israel.

Qatar “has not allowed the prisoners to meet or speak with their families or with officials handling their cases,” General Bagherzadeh wrote. He called on the Red Cross to meet with the pilots, investigate their condition, and facilitate their release as soon as possible.

Aaron Boxerman contributed reporting.

item.title: No Way Out
item.description:
Donald Trump won election promising to deport millions of immigrants. Many dismissed that as campaign talk. But 19 months after taking office, the administration is as determined as ever to reach its targets.

Federal immigration agents have been arresting roughly 2,000 people a day. (Last week we also learned about a plan for ICE agents to get gloves that can deliver electric shocks.) Billions are being spent on new detention centers.

And around the world, the U.S. is paying developing countries, from El Salvador to Rwanda, to take deportees off its hands. Today, my colleague Nicholas Casey writes about how America is creating a system of indefinite detention abroad.

By Nicholas Casey

As he stepped out of the American military cargo plane, Roberto Mosquera had no idea where he was or why he had been taken there. He had never heard of a country called Eswatini.

The tiny, landlocked country in southern Africa, until recently called Swaziland, is one of at least 35 countries — including South Sudan, Ghana, Palau, Uzbekistan and Moldova — that have made deals with the U.S. to take deportees from other countries of origin.

Mosquera arrived in the U.S. on a fishing boat from Cuba in 1980, when he was 12. In his 20s, he took a plea deal and served time in prison after shooting a rival gangster in the leg. That would have been grounds to deport him, but Cuba wasn’t cooperating, so Mosquera was allowed to stay. He built a new life for himself, becoming a plumber and a born-again Christian; he married and had four daughters.

But all that changed last year when he went to renew his work permit. An immigration official told him that his time in America was up. After stints in U.S. detention centers, he was flown to Eswatini, where he’s being held in the country’s maximum-security prison with four other detainees from Jamaica, Laos, Yemen and Vietnam.

The Trump administration is building a growing detention archipelago overseas, often in unstable or autocratic countries. And in cases like Mosquera’s, it’s turning deportation into a form of indefinite imprisonment with no legal recourse.

“Can I ask you a question?” Mosquera asked me on a WhatsApp video call in June, using a phone he obtained after a hunger strike. “Do you think I’ll ever get out of here?”

‘Depraved monsters’

The first time the Trump administration paid a foreign government to take deportees was last year, in a deal with the autocratic president of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele.

Bukele accepted a $6 million payment to hold some 250 Venezuelan immigrants in a megaprison. The Venezuelans were later flown home, but many claimed that they were abused and tortured by their prison guards.

Since then, variations of this deal have multiplied. Many of the countries that have agreed to take deportees are unstable, or desperate for American cash. The Central African Republic is in the middle of a civil war. The Democratic Republic of Congo took 15 deportees shortly before the recent Ebola outbreak. Eswatini, which received $5.1 million in its arrangement with the Trump administration, is one of the world’s last absolute monarchies.

At home, the administration has justified its actions by casting those sent abroad as inhuman.

In a post on X, the Department of Homeland Security had called Mosquera and the four other men who were sent to Eswatini with him “depraved monsters” who were “so uniquely barbaric their home countries refuse to take them back.”

‘No way out’

The deportations — whether they involve immigrants with criminal histories or not — often happen before deportees can argue their cases before a judge.

And because they are foreign nationals, with no legal status in the countries to which they have been sent, they generally remain under indefinite detention abroad, without charges and with little or no recourse in any court of law.

As a result, for some detainees, there is no clear path to get out. They remain in the third countries to which they are sent, stuck in a legal purgatory. They are a new class of prisoner created by America’s widening crackdown on immigration.

More than a year after his arrival, Mosquera still sits in that same maximum-security prison. No charges have been brought against him. He has no way to appeal his predicament. And there is no sign that he will ever be released from prison. “It’s like you wake up, and you’re in this place, and there’s no way out,” his lawyer said.

In 2024, when Trump again set his sights on the White House, Mosquera saw himself as one of the working-class Americans whom Trump said he would defend. Mosquera’s sister told me she remembered Mosquera practically stumping for Trump. “He would sit on the patio and say, ‘Trump is going to change everything, you’ll see,’” she said.

Three more groups of men have landed in Eswatini since Mosquera arrived. He has a job now: showing new arrivals how to get money wired from home, where to wash their clothes, what to do when the power goes out.

The guards have been clearing space for more detainees.

Read the full story.

Sweida is the only Syrian province that is still resisting the authority of the central government. It is home to the Druse minority, many of whom are wary of the post-Assad authorities after sectarian clashes last year. My colleagues traveled to the province and spoke to residents who fear that violence could erupt again.

Four Renaissance paintings were stolen from a museum in Sicily, Italy, in a brazen heist.

Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and close adviser, met with Hamas leaders in Egypt to try to advance Trump’s plan for the future of Gaza.

The U.S. and Iran are poised to miss today’s deadline to end the war and rein in Iran’s nuclear program. There’s no end in sight.

Syria said it had arrested a former police chief who was convicted in Austria for crimes committed during the country’s civil war.

At least 93 patients have tested positive for cholera in Yangon, Myanmar, an outbreak that has been attributed to poor sanitation.

Tropical Storm Lala pummeled Hawaii with heavy rains. Officials warned of potentially life-threatening flooding.

At least 47 people were killed in Indonesia after it was rocked by a 7.7-magnitude earthquake on Saturday.

A shooting at the U.S. consulate in Toronto has exposed an underground guns-for-hire network.

Bou Meng, a Cambodian painter and rare survivor of the Khmer Rouge torture house, died. He was 85.

Selena Gomez, the actress, singer and beauty mogul, has been accused in a lawsuit of defrauding investors in her mental health start-up.

Jeff Bezos is buying a piece of Liverpool Football Club, his first known investment into a sports team.

The most clicked link in your newsletter on Friday was about Pakistan’s electric motorcycles.

Football: Cristiano Ronaldo said he will “probably” retire next summer and plans to have “more fun.”

Running: Finland’s Alisa Vainio and Amanal Petros of Germany set European Championship records in the women’s and men’s marathons.

When the police chief learned last week that workers had found gold sealed inside a small brick cellar below a defunct brewery in Belgium, he was sure it was a prank. But then he saw the proof: 49 gold bars and more than 4,000 coins, a cache worth an estimated $10 million, its origin unknown. Who will get to keep it?

VHS Dates, an Instagram account with nearly 900,000 followers, is about videos of people looking for romance in the 1980s and ’90s. Many viewers say they have been genuinely touched by the clips. “How would it feel to be in love?” asked a middle-aged man named Doug in one. “I would really, really, really like to know.”

Intrigued, a Times reporter set up an interview with the people behind the account. At the meeting, they had a confession: The dating videos weren’t from decades ago. They were staged. See how convincing some were.

On the banks of the River Krishna in southeastern India, on what was once banana groves and vegetable fields, there’s a new city taking shape. The planners hope it will be the city of India’s future.

Building Amaravati as the new capital city for Andhra Pradesh, a state of 50 million people, is an enormous task: More than 25,000 people are working at the site on any given day. Sixty percent of the new city is expected to be covered by water or green space, complete with bike lanes and a technology hub worth hundreds of millions of dollars. Meet the man behind the most ambitious city-building project in modern India.

Plan: If you missed last week’s eclipse in Europe, don’t worry. You can catch a blockbuster eclipse next year.

Listen: Here are five classical music albums to enjoy right now.

Watch: The documentary “American Doctor” focuses on a planned medical trip to Gaza by U.S. physicians. It’s a critic’s pick.

Hunt: Which Manhattan apartment would you buy for $600,000?

Thicker than a crepe but lighter than a pancake, baghrir is enjoyed for breakfast across Northern Africa. Instead of the usual topping of melted butter and honey, this version calls for date syrup and salted yogurt.

Where are these hot springs?

Uunartoq, Greenland

Sajama, Bolivia

Song-Köl, Kyrgyzstan

Arkhangai, Mongolia

Here are today’s Spelling Bee, Mini Crossword, Wordle and Sudoku. Find all our games here.

That’s it for today. See you tomorrow! — Katrin

Nicholas Casey was our guest writer today.

We welcome your feedback. Send us your suggestions at theworld@nytimes.com.

item.title: Canadian Petition to Expel U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra Takes Off
item.description:
After boycotting American products and shunning vacations south of the border, Canadians in their thousands are pouring their incandescent anger at the United States into a new cause: ousting the American ambassador.

More than 160,000 people have signed a petition to the Canadian Parliament, submitted by a Calgary resident on July 21, calling for the removal of the ambassador, Pete Hoekstra.

The petition asserts that Mr. Hoekstra, a faithful messenger of President Trump’s aggressive stance toward Canada, has harmed U.S.-Canada relations. The two countries are locked in a trade war, and their relationship, once the closest two nations can be, has been at a historic low since Mr. Trump retook office.

Just 500 signatures are legally required to bring an online petition to the Parliament floor for discussion, and this one will most likely be put forward for debate in the fall by Elizabeth May, the leader of Canada’s Green Party.

The petition lays out the reasoning for Mr. Hoekstra’s removal: it argues that he has “normalized the Trump administration’s threats to annex Canada as the 51st state.” Mr. Hoekstra has reposted Mr. Trump’s 51st-state jabs on social media and has dismissed Canadians’ anger at the rhetoric as “emotional” and inexplicable.

It also states that Mr. Hoekstra has interfered in Canadian politics in a manner “inconsistent with diplomatic protocol.” It lays out how activists from Alberta seeking to break away from the rest of the country repeatedly met with State Department officials, “raising serious questions about U.S. diplomatic interference in Canadian unity.”

The petition calls on the Canadian government to invoke the Vienna Convention of Diplomatic Relations, the international accord that governs diplomacy, declare Mr. Hoekstra “persona non grata” and request his removal from office, as well as to set up a parliamentary committee to review “U.S. diplomatic interference in Canadian domestic affairs."

The United States Embassy in Ottawa referred questions to the State Department, which did not respond to a request for comment.

The petition culminates months of souring public sentiment toward Mr. Hoekstra personally, mirroring the plummeting views toward the United States generally.

Polling shows Canadians’ opinion of the United States has rapidly gotten worse since Mr. Trump took office and began targeting Canada with tariffs and talk of making it part of the United States. A Pew survey published in June found that only 35 percent of Canadians now view the United States as a reliable partner, down sharply from 2022, when it was 82 percent. Canadian recreational visits to the United States have shrunk by more than a quarter over the past year.

In this context, Mr. Hoekstra, a former Republican Representative from Michigan, has become notorious in Canada for his blunt, unapologetic tone, which channels Mr. Trump’s.

One comment that drew ire came in November, when Mr. Hoekstra was asked if he understood why Canadians found Mr. Trump’s 51st state remarks upsetting.

“Here, I’ll just get myself in trouble,” he said. “I go around the country and people will say, ‘Pete, you just don’t understand why we’re so mad about the 51st state.’ Yeah, you’re right. I don’t.”

Unlike some of his colleagues, Mr. Hoekstra has never been summoned by the Canadian government, a step taken when a diplomatic emissary is seen as overstepping so badly that the host government needs to give them a talking-to.

The United States ambassador to France, Charles Kushner, the father of Mr. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared, has been twice summoned by the French government over comments he has made about French domestic affairs. The U.S. ambassador to Belgium was also summoned for comments he made.

Mr. Hoekstra also raised eyebrows when he invited the right-wing populist activist Tamara Lich, who had been convicted of organizing the trucker convoy that wreaked havoc in Ottawa for a month in 2022, to this year’s 4th of July party at the ambassador’s official residence.

Mr. Hoekstra has been accused of political interference in another nation’s domestic affairs. In 2020, while serving as U.S. ambassador to the Netherlands in the first Trump administration, he hosted an event at the U.S. embassy with a nativist, anti-immigrant Dutch party.

Expelling a U.S. ambassador would be a first for Canada, but far from unprecedented globally.

American ambassadors have been expelled during major geopolitical crises in the past, including during the Cold War, both World Wars, as well as more recently during crises with Latin American countries such as Venezuela.

Mr. Hoekstra’s stance in Canada aligns with the U.S. administration’s foreign policy elsewhere. The State Department has made significant efforts to cultivate and promote identarian politics in Europe through visits and senior official meetings with European political parties and other organizations sharing these ideas, including in Germany and Britain.

Representatives of the business community said Mr. Hoekstra had been a solid interlocutor during tumultuous times for the relationship between the two nations.

The U.S. Embassy in Canada recommended speaking to some business leaders about their working relationship with Mr. Hoekstra. They included Rick Tachuk, president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Canada, a private, nonprofit membership organization promoting trade and investment across the border; and Beth Burke, chief executive of the Canadian American Business Council, a nonprofit, nonpartisan group.

Mr. Tachuk says that Mr. Hoekstra has been available to business leaders and cares about the U.S.-Canada trade relationship.

“He at times can be blunt, but, in many respects, that is an advantage for us because he helps articulate the view of the president, and helps us understand what the challenges are,” Mr. Tachuk said in an interview on Friday.

“Ambassador Hoekstra has to deliver some very unpopular messages here in Canada. It’s a tough job but he’s doing his best,” he added.

Ms. Burke said Mr. Hoekstra was well connected across the administration and an effective messenger.

“I also really value knowing where you stand in a situation. Sometimes pleasantries and diplomatic speak muddy the waters,” she added.

item.title: With Priests Scarce in Rural Italy, an African Pastor Is Filling the Void
item.description:
The priest stepped into the bedroom where his 90-year-old parishioner lay sleeping in a hospital bed, flanked by oxygen tanks. The pastor towered over the bed and leaned down to move close to the patient, Carlo Martini, as the old man’s eyes fluttered open briefly.

“How are you?” the priest, the Rev. Vincent Souly, asked, a bit too loudly.

Mr. Martini’s wife, Renza Giagnoni, stood to the side and watched. “It looks like we’re the United Nations!” she said, also a bit too loudly.

Father Souly is one of the few Black faces in the province of Prato, a mountainous region of Tuscany, in central Italy, where he has served for 15 years as a Roman Catholic priest. He has built warm relationships with his predominantly Italian flocks and is embraced by many parishioners. Born in Burkina Faso, and raised and ordained in the Ivory Coast, he is now an Italian citizen and is committed to staying in Prato as long as he is needed. Yet, he said, his Italian passport does not necessarily make others see him as Italian.

“Where I’m from, we say, ‘A piece of wood, no matter how long it stays in water, will never become a crocodile,’” he said. “You’re accepted, up to a point. But there’s this unspoken part, right? You remain what you are.”

He felt a flash of that otherness when Ms. Giagnoni referred to the United Nations, he told us later, or when parishioners referred to him as a “prete di colore” or “priest of color.”

He would prefer that people refer to him by his country of origin rather than by the color of his skin, he said. “When you say, ‘He is an African priest,’ it’s already more elegant, it’s more cultured,” he said. “That means that you’ve tried to locate where Africa is on the world map. If you say, ‘He is from the Ivory Coast,’ that’s even better. Using the color is a shortcut.”

As fewer Italians take the vows of priesthood, Father Souly is among about 1,130 African priests who oversee Italian churches — approximately 4 percent of Italy’s clergy, not including more junior church positions.

Father Souly is part of a historic wave of immigration that is changing Europe. Roughly one in seven people in the European Union was born outside their country of residence, the highest rate since the bloc started compiling such statistics nearly two decades ago. Italy, with 12 percent born overseas, has one of the largest immigrant populations on the continent — a remarkable reversal for a nation that once helped to fuel mass emigration to America.

The priest’s life highlights a nuance of that changing Italy. In the common consciousness, immigrants are typically filling labor shortages in the country’s many depopulated and aging communities — mainly across the agricultural, manufacturing and service sectors, and often on the peripheries of Italian life.

Yet Father Souly is helping to shore up an institution at the heart of Italian history and national identity — the Roman Catholic Church. Unlike foreigners working on the sidelines of Italian society, Father Souly stands front and center in his community. He is there out of spiritual mission rather than economic desperation. And his work helps sustain his parishioners’ religious lives, even if some of them feel ambivalent about the implications of his presence.

Weekends find Father Souly — a tall, gentle man with a quiet smile — careering around mountain roads in a 19-year-old silver Fiat hatchback as he races between churches and Masses.

On the weekend we visited, he conducted services in two villages on a Saturday afternoon before holding a happy hour at his rectory, hosting several couples for Prosecco and beer, and potato chips piled on paper plates. In the evening, he attended a pizza dinner at a social club run by one of his parishes. The following morning, he led Mass at three churches before noon, delivering three distinct homilies that he said he had improvised on the spot, before spending the afternoon visiting families across his district.

“Giving reason to our hope will be a fight every day,” he said in one homily. “It will be strained by many things every day.”

Throughout the weekend, his parishioners spoke of him with clear warmth.

Gabriela Tabusso Morini, one of the guests at the happy hour, recalled first meeting Father Souly as he hoed the garden outside a church near her home. Days later, he saw Ms. Morini and her husband at Mass and welcomed them by name. “This struck us so much, that he remembered us,” she said. “We weren’t just any old faces, we were people.”

Yet for all of his popularity, Father Souly still feels a sense of loneliness.

“We are all isolated, each in his own world,” he said, standing in the rectory kitchen after finishing the Sunday Masses. He stirred simmering pots of carp and chicken stews — both recipes that his mother had taught him how to cook. Slicing cucumbers, avocado and red onion for a salad, he said that he shopped for special ingredients like cow hooves and a West African variant of eggplant at shops run by immigrants from China or Pakistan.

Occasionally, people ask him when he intends to return to the Ivory Coast. Some ask because they hope he will never leave, he said. Others “ask when you’ll go home because they are looking for confirmation that you are, indeed, going home one day.”

Father Souly is the third of six children of a cook and a homemaker in western Ivory Coast. As a child, he said, he never imagined that he would travel so far from home. He entered seminary when he was 18 and was ordained at 32. In 2007, when he was 35, he received a Vatican scholarship to pursue a master’s degree in canon law in Rome.

He landed in Italy speaking only French and Mooré, an official language of Burkina Faso, and got lost on the way from the airport to his dormitory. For the first three months after he arrived in Rome, he took intensive grammar classes for seven hours a day, he added, and once he started his academic degree, he continued classes with nuns and priests from across Africa, Eastern Europe and a few from China.

Although his scholarship covered tuition, he struggled to pay for room and board. He took a job as an assistant pastor in northern Italy, eventually transferring to a similar post at one of the four parishes where he is now the main priest. After receiving his doctorate in 2014, he decided against returning to the Ivory Coast.

Local residents, who had gone without a priest for some years, helped to furnish the rectory where he lived and bought him a bed to accommodate his lanky frame.

Parishioners have varied recollections of how they felt about him when he first arrived.

According to Maria Lucarini, 41, the mayor of Vernio, the village that hosts Father Souly’s largest parish, “He had to work a bit because, after all, this is a mountain community, not used to seeing — maybe at the beginning when he arrived — many people of color.”

“When people got to know the person and saw how much he commits himself to the community, maybe that initial barrier of his different skin color collapsed,” Ms. Lucarini added.

Ilaria Tonini, 46, said that an Italian priest, born and raised in the area, “would certainly be better,” as the community had previously been accustomed to a locally born pastor who had served for over 30 years. But she praised Father Souly because he “really fit right in.”

Others had less complicated memories. Father Souly’s heritage “didn’t make any difference,” said Osanna Becherini, 79, after a recent Saturday afternoon Mass. “Religion is religion. Rightly so, white, Black or yellow,” she said. “What’s important is that he is present. He baptized all my grandchildren.”

Because of the changing demographics, a handful of Father Souly’s congregants are also from Africa. Lena Ehika, 37, moved from Nigeria five years ago to join her husband, a factory worker in the region. She said it “doesn’t make any difference to me” that she and Father Souly came from the same continent.

“Most of the Masses I’ve attended here are celebrated by Black priests,” she noted.

Some parishioners are so accommodating that it can be hard for foreign priests to return to their home countries at the end of a posting, said the Rev. Cyril Arnaud Meba, 35, a Cameroonian who assists Father Souly during Masses.

“Here we can find people who welcome us, generous people, people who give us so many things. And then we get used to receiving this, and then we don’t want to return anymore because it feels good to live here,” said Father Meba, who said he was nevertheless determined to return to Cameroon. “We all have a good life.”

Still, Father Souly said that some Italians looked down on him because he came from a poorer part of the world. They did not realize, he said, that they were often spiritually impoverished — having lost touch with their extended families and having forgone human companionship for digital media.

“There is material poverty, and there is spiritual, intellectual and cultural poverty,” Father Souly said. “But explaining that in a place like this is difficult. The fact of having electricity, these roads, the development, the modernity — they think that is enough to say, ‘I am better than you.’”

Father Souly’s biggest challenge is spending enough time in his various parishes.

At every Mass, rows of empty pews outnumber filled benches. Yet the remaining churchgoers still struggle to get his attention before he races off to the next village. His focus is divided even further by his duties as the head canonical legal officer for the diocese.

“Before, apparently, the priest who actually lived right in the town knew everyone,” said Pietro D’Amore, 42, who owns a second home near one of Father Souly’s churches. Mr. D’Amore’s eldest son serves as an altar boy, but he lamented that he saw the priest only during Mass “and then he has to rush away.”

Father Souly does his best. He has tried to visit every member of every church at their home, he said.

At the pizza dinner hosted by the parish social club recently, he sat at the center of a long table surrounded by those who had attended Mass an hour earlier. Ms. Lucarini, the mayor, sat across from him with her husband and young daughter, who had brought a sketchbook. Father Souly tried to show an interest in what the girl was doing, but she barely seemed to pay attention to him before producing a drawing of a smiling brown man wearing glasses and a priest’s collar.

The next day, Father Souly shuttled from house to house throughout the afternoon. He visited a sexton and his wife to check on preparations for a first confession ceremony. As he left Mr. Martini’s sickbed, Ms. Giagnoni tried, multiple times, to persuade him to take a zuccherino, a traditional sugar cookie, until he finally explained that he was pre-diabetic and should not eat sweets.

Father Souly dropped by the home of Sara Orlandi, 46, a legal secretary, and her husband, Alessandro Ballotti, 57, who manages a mechanics’ shop.

They warmly greeted Father Souly and invited him to stay for dinner. When he politely turned them down, telling them that he planned to visit a cancer patient in another village, Ms. Orlandi gently ribbed him.

“Give me a break,” Ms. Orlandi joked. “Who are you, the pope?” Mr. Ballotti asked Father Souly to come back the following week to watch a soccer match, but the priest said he would not have time.

Father Souly, perched on a couch, told them that he hoped the bishop would soon send an Italian-born priest to help him serve the parishes.

“Keep coming to us once in a while, please, even if there’s a change,” Ms. Orlandi said.

Later, Father Souly said that he believed it would help to work with a native Italian partner. People would always think of him as foreign, he said.

“It’s remained in people’s minds,” he said. “It’s difficult to remove it.”

When I moved to Rome, a Ghanian priest I met in an Italian class pointed out a quiet shift: with fewer Italian-born men entering the priesthood, African pastors were increasingly stepping in to shepherd parishes across the country, not just study theology or canon law.Curious about their day-to-day reality, we shadowed Rev. Vincent Souly over a weekend. He opened his life to us — from presiding over Masses and making home visits to reflecting on the burden of serving a community where his heritage can complicate his welcome.

item.title: A Consulate Shooting, a Toronto Street and a Network of Guns for Hire
item.description:
The apartment towers on Martha Eaton Way loom over an urban creek in north Toronto, a working-class part of the city where ethnic stores dominate the strip malls.

Violent episodes have cast a long shadow over the neighborhood, known as “Creek” to the young people for whom the address can confer clout. Some remember that an 8-year-old boy was killed by a stray bullet through his bedroom window last summer, and that a teenager was fatally shot at the pizza shop next door a year before that.

Others are too young to know that an adjacent street is named after a Toronto police officer killed there decades ago, or that a gang from this neighborhood played a defining role in the city’s bloody “summer of the gun” in 2005.

Crime is broadly low in Toronto, with homicides and car theft rates dropping over the last year. But a recent spate of shootings has put many on edge, including synagogues and Jewish schools and storefronts that have been targeted by gunfire.

Then, in March, two gunmen fired at the U.S. Consulate in the heart of Toronto’s downtown; a stark, low-rise structure on a busy avenue dotted with court offices, university buildings and hospitals.

Security cameras showed the gunmen taking turns to fire the same weapon at the building. Hunting for them, investigators zeroed in on the three apartment towers on Martha Eaton Way. Their investigation took a tragic turn in June, when a police officer trying to carry out a search warrant inside one of the buildings was shot dead.

The violence depicts an emerging trend, the police say, of criminals using encrypted apps to anonymously recruit teenagers into what investigators call a guns-for-hire network, treating young people as gig workers in the underworld economy.

Then, in late July, the U.S. Consulate was fired on again. The suspects, arrested in early August, were two other teenagers who the police believe were involved with the network.

Explosive bangs and shouting jolted Mario Kramo awake in his fourth-floor apartment in one of the Martha Eaton Way towers just before sunrise on June 11. In the hallway, police officers tried to resuscitate a wounded officer.

“I realized that they definitely came for a raid,” Mr. Kramo said. “And it went badly.”

Next door, his neighbor, Nicholas Bennett, 19, fired a single gunshot, the police say, that killed Constable Marc Pinizzotto, 43. Constable Pinizzotto, a veteran of an elite task force, was part of a high-risk takedown unit dispatched to arrest Mr. Bennett that morning.

Mr. Bennett was accused of participating in a few of the roughly two dozen shootings at homes and businesses across the city linked to the guns-for-hire network, according to police and court documents.

Two other teenagers who lived in the building, both wanted in the U.S. Consulate shooting, tried to flee.

The police apprehended the first, Sheldon Tracey-Stewart, 18, in the neighborhood carrying, they said, a loaded Glock 17 handgun. The other, Zara Jabbi, 19, fled and a week later was arrested at Toronto’s main airport.

Criminals typically avoid filming themselves in the act to avoid creating evidence. But in the guns-for-hire network, video recordings are a condition of payment for picking up a “contract,” said Chief Superintendent Joe Matthews, who is leading the investigation.

But the promised payment — in the hundreds or thousands of dollars, depending on the job — sometimes doesn’t materialize.

“They’re now facing potential jail time for something they didn’t even get paid for,” said Superintendent Matthews, who grew up near Martha Eaton Way.

The guns-for-hire network is spread across Toronto and the surrounding areas, and involves a few dozen young people, the police said.

Earlier this month, the police announced the arrest of Xen-Ul-Abdeen Syed, 19, of Brampton, Ontario, and a 15-year-old who cannot be named because of a youth publication ban, who were allegedly involved in the network.

Europol, the European police agency, has said it is investigating a similar trend of youth hired on social media to commit violent acts, including homicides, in a “violence-as-a-service” scheme that is “accessible, scalable and driven by online ecosystems” across borders. One of the most prolific contractors of violence in Europe is a criminal network with links to Iran, according to an investigation by the BBC.

In Canada, questions about the network’s possible financiers have emerged following a criminal complaint filed in New York in May. According to the complaint, the F.B.I. says a 32-year-old man was heard in a secretly recorded call taking responsibility for the consulate attack and one at a synagogue, in the name of a militant group that serves as a proxy for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

Britain designated that group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyya, a terrorist organization in July. Canada’s public safety ministry did not respond to questions about whether it plans to do the same.

Three other arrests have been made in connection with synagogue shootings in Toronto, but the police are still investigating links to the guns-for-hire network.

“In Canada we have our guys,” said the man heard on the wiretap, Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, according to the complaint. Neither Canadian authorities nor the F.B.I. have disclosed who dispatched the young shooters, who the police do not believe were ideologically motivated.

Monte MacGregor, a defense lawyer representing one of the teenagers accused in the consulate shooting, said it was telling that the police did not file terrorism charges.

His client was asserting his innocence, Mr. MacGregor said, adding that for whoever was involved: “It speaks to the level of sophistication and understanding of the actual people pulling the trigger. It’s probably fairly low.”

The recruitment over social media has set the network apart from past cases, said Andrew Hammond, president of the Organization for National Gang Information and Awareness, a Canadian nonprofit.

Previously, older gang members groomed young recruits through lower-stakes crimes, like petty theft or stashing firearms, to build trust and loyalty. Social media has upended that model, and gives higher-ranking gang members more anonymity, said Sergeant Hammond, a Toronto detective who is not involved in this case.

The trend has grown more pronounced in the last two years, he said, and other Canadian cities, including Montreal, have seen versions of it, what experts there call the “disposable army.”

On the afternoon of Constable Pinizzotto’s death, a neighborhood youth group gathered for its weekly activities, sports and snacks. The news jarred the older teenagers.

“For some young people, it’s another day on the block,” said Destin Bujang, executive director of the Black Creek Youth Initiative. One of the alleged consulate shooters had long dropped in on the program, which is often paid for out of Mr. Bujang’s own pocket, he said, amid unreliable public funding and cutbacks in city programming, which hit underprivileged neighborhoods the hardest.

Some of the group’s participants would say they want to provide for their family, “whatever it takes,” Mr. Bujang said.

Toronto gangs are also exploiting that pressure to recruit boys to travel across the country, as far north as Nunavut, to sell drugs, the police and social services workers say.

When they see alerts about missing boys in the neighborhood, Josiah Sappleton-Stout and Grace Garawai, both 17, say their first guess is the boy has “gone O.T.”, or out-of-town, to sell drugs.

“Because we’re from the hood, not everyone here is rich,” said Ms. Garawai, a high-school athlete on a local basketball court. “I feel like if you get into that situation, it’s unintentional. It kind of just happens.”

The lure of money — young people posting stacks of $20 bills on social media — can be hard to escape, said Mr. Sappleton-Stout, who is enrolled in a trades apprenticeship program. Gesturing at the court, he said, “Adding little things like this makes a big contribution to the community. It keeps kids out of trouble.”

Not every young person on Martha Eaton Way has been so lucky.

Just before the first day of school in September 2024, Mario Giddings, 15, was shot outside the pizza shop next to the building where the raids in June took place. His killers have not been caught.

“It’s still there, fresh, in my blood, in my eyes, seeing him just walk out that door and never return,” said Fortunata Giddings, Mario’s aunt and primary caregiver in Canada. Ms. Giddings, an airport cleaner, said her nephew would inexplicably come home with expensive clothes. He died, she said, in $400 sneakers.

For nearly a decade covering crime in Toronto, I’ve watched gangs exploit youth and the leniency of the youth justice system. But social media has fundamentally reshaped how these kids are recruited, a shift exposed after the shootings at the U.S. consulate. As I continue tracking this story, I invite anyone with experience, information, or expertise in Canadian youth criminal justice to reach out at vjosa.isai@nytimes.com.

item.title: Kushner Meets With Hamas to Advance Trump’s Gaza Plan
item.description:
Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and close adviser, met with Hamas leaders in Egypt on Sunday, two Hamas officials and another official briefed on the meetings said. The talks were part of a diplomatic push to advance Mr. Trump’s plan for the future of Gaza.

A U.S. official confirmed that Mr. Kushner was in Egypt for talks on Gaza, without providing further details. All four officials spoke on the condition of anonymity to detail Mr. Kushner’s meetings.

Mr. Kushner’s visit to the Middle East comes as the U.S.-backed plan to disarm Hamas has appeared to hit a dead end. Last month, Mr. Trump announced that his Board of Peace had reached an agreement with Hamas that aimed to strip the Palestinian group of its weapons.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel later said he rejected the deal, appearing to put it on ice. After the meetings with Hamas on Sunday, Mr. Kushner was expected to travel to Israel to meet with Mr. Netanyahu to discuss the situation in Gaza.

Direct talks between the U.S. government and Hamas, which the United States has designated as a terrorist organization, were once rare. But the Trump administration broke that taboo, holding multiple rounds of negotiations with the group to win freedom for the hostages Hamas seized in Israel and to end the Israeli military campaign in Gaza.

Though Mr. Kushner does not hold an official U.S. government position, Mr. Trump has tapped him, alongside real estate developer Steve Witkoff, to lead diplomacy on matters as diverse as Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Israel-Hamas war.

Disarming Hamas is a key component of the president’s 20-point plan for the Palestinian enclave, much of which is still unrealized nearly a year after an initial cease-fire was reached last October. But many Israelis are skeptical of the Trump administration’s proposal and say it is unlikely to actually compel Hamas to give up its weapons.

For the deal with Hamas to go ahead, Israel would also most likely have to agree to a phased timeline for withdrawing its forces from the Gaza Strip in parallel with Hamas gradually handing over its weapons. Mr. Netanyahu has been loath to do so, demanding “genuine disarmament” before any Israeli withdrawals.

Analysts said the Israeli prime minister’s position reflected the country’s hawkish turn after the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks that ignited the two-year war in Gaza. Mr. Netanyahu’s efforts to appeal to voters ahead of national elections this fall also were a factor, they said.

Neither Mr. Kushner nor Hamas publicly discussed their meeting in Egypt.

Hamas said a delegation of senior officials led by Khalil al-Hayya, Hamas’s political chief, had arrived in Egypt to meet with “mediators and guarantors” of the Gaza cease-fire talks. The group said it was committed to Mr. Trump’s peace framework, which it accused Israel of undermining by continuing to bombard the enclave despite the truce.

Israel has “escalated militarily on the ground and deepened the humanitarian catastrophe, even as it explicitly rejected the road map,” Hamas said in a statement.

Egypt’s president, Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, met with Mr. Kushner to discuss the Gaza peace process, among other issues, according to a statement from the president’s s office.

Adam Rasgon contributed reporting.

item.title: Liechtenstein Changes Its Law to Allow Women to Ascend the Throne
item.description:
Of the roughly four dozen countries where royal families reign, two have wrestled this summer with questions of gender and succession in the modern era, taking starkly different approaches.

Liechtenstein, a tiny nation of about 40,000 people wedged between Switzerland and Austria in the Alps, took one route: On Saturday, it announced that women would now be able to become the monarch and wield the broad political power of the throne.

The Princely House of Liechtenstein said in a statement that it was shifting from male-only succession to absolute primogeniture, making the future firstborn child of the ruling royal family heir to the throne, regardless of gender.

“With this legislative amendment, we wish to ensure that both the Principality of Liechtenstein and the Princely House are governed by the person best prepared for this task,” said Hereditary Prince Alois, the country’s de facto leader. The sons and daughters of the reigning royal “are familiarized from their youth with the unique characteristics of the Principality and the Princely House,” and will “in principle,” be best suited for the ruling role, he said.

Prince Alois, 58, is the son of the reigning Prince Hans-Adam, 81, and he has for more than two decades served as his father’s deputy, handling the duties of head of state in his place. He is a father of four, with an elder son, a daughter and two younger sons, but the rule change does not apply to them or anyone already born. It will apply to all future births, Prince Alois told the local news media.

Liechtenstein’s move to adopt equal succession rights puts it in the majority among nearby nations with royal families.

Sweden, the Netherlands, Norway and Belgium adopted absolute primogeniture in the late 20th century, and Denmark, Luxembourg and Britain followed suit soon after, giving women equal succession rights.

Still, Liechtenstein’s decision is notable because it comes just weeks after Japan’s legislature took a different approach to royal succession amid a looming crisis.

The imperial family in Japan is now made up of only 16 people: five men and 11 women. This summer, the government advanced a proposal to allow this dwindling clan to adopt distant male relatives, in an effort to help ensure the survival of the world’s oldest monarchy, which only allows men to ascend the throne.

The proposal was supported by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, a conservative who last year became the first woman to lead Japan. But it angered many who saw this supposed workaround as unnecessary and argued that the country should instead allow women to reign as empress.

Members of the Japanese imperial family appear to have some reservations about the idea themselves. Asked about the proposal last week, Crown Prince Akishino, the younger brother of Emperor Naruhito, and the next in line for the throne, said he could not talk about the decision because he was constrained by his position. But he acknowledged that he had mixed feelings.

When it comes to serving in imperial roles, the crown prince said, “I believe there is no difference between men and women,” according to The Associated Press. He added, “Society needs to keep making progress, and I believe it is important for people with different views to keep thinking what’s best.”

item.title: Thieves Steal Four Renaissance Paintings From Italian Museum in Brazen Heist
item.description:
Four paintings by the Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Messina, Sicily, on Saturday, Italian officials said.

Taking advantage of an annual religious celebration that brings tens of thousands to Messina’s streets, thieves made off with three of five panels that constitute the Polyptych of San Gregorio as well as a small double-sided devotional painting. They are the only works by Antonello da Messina, commonly called Antonello, that remained in his native city.

The celebration, the Procession of the Vara, is a religious ritual that takes places every Aug. 15. Some 100,000 people attended the celebration and the city’s law enforcement officials were focused on maintaining order there, city officials said. “Coinciding with la Vara, it was certainly a planned theft,” Mayor Federico Basile said in a telephone interview.

Commissioned in the 15th century for the church of San Gregorio, which was destroyed during a devastating earthquake in 1908, the San Gregorio altarpiece originally consisted of six panels. Only five remain and were housed at Messina’s Accascina Regional Museum.

The thieves initially took all five remaining panels, but left two behind near a fence outside the museum, perhaps in their haste to escape, Mr. Basile said. The mayor said that passers-by noticed “suspicious activity” at the museum and immediately alerted the police.

Vincenzo Caruso, Messina’s chief cultural official, said that the thieves smashed a sealed case to get to the other work they stole, a small double-sided panel that depicts the Madonna and Child with a Franciscan friar on one side, and Christ on the other.

He said police were reviewing security camera footage from inside and outside the museum to look for clues. “From what I understand some people saw the theft and hopefully they took photographs,” he said.

Mr. Caruso said interest in Antonello spiked this year after the Italian government bought a painting by the artist for $15 million.

An official with Italy’s art theft squad said investigations had begun but declined to provide further details. On Friday, Italians celebrated the recovery of three artworks that had been stolen from a museum near Parma earlier this year.

Antonello is considered one of the Renaissance’s great artists and is known for his mastery of portraiture. There are only some 40 works definitively attributed to him, said Grazia Musolino, an art historian who curated a recent catalog about him. “He made a crucial contribution to the Renaissance by unifying two very important aspects of Renaissance art: the work of Flemish artists and Italian art,” she said.

The two works were the only paintings by Antonello to remain in the city where he was born around 1430 and where he lived on and off until his death there in 1479. The larger work is signed and dated 1473. The double-sided panel was created slightly earlier and was bought by the Sicilian Region at a Sotheby’s auction in 2003.

The theft is a blow to the city. Mr. Basile, the mayor, said that for the past few years the city has focused on the “Messina, City of Antonello” brand and was moving forward with a plan to create a virtual museum in Antonello’s home.

“Antonello is the greatest ambassador of our city because he has Messina in his name,” said Mr. Caruso.

Experts said that works stolen from museums are notoriously difficult to sell. Francesco Finocchiaro, the coordinator of Archeoclub d’Italia in Sicily, a cultural heritage association, said his fear was that “intermediaries and unscrupulous collectors could be behind the theft of works of this significance.”

Marisa Mercurio, the director of the museum, declined to be interviewed, but told Sky News Italia that the museum’s alarms and security systems were operational and guards were present. “It’s not true that there was no security,” she said.

item.title: As Iran War Turns Into Economic Battle, a New U.S. Strategy Recalls Old Ones
item.description:
President Trump’s cease-fire with Iran in June envisioned a broader deal to end the war and rein in the country’s nuclear program, all negotiated within 60 days.

But that deadline, set to pass on Monday, has been essentially abandoned, and the war has transformed into a contest of willpower and economic endurance that has no end in sight.

There have been no publicly reported U.S. strikes on Iranian targets since late July. Yet the effective collapse of the agreement underscores how Mr. Trump has struggled to end the war he started in February alongside Israel, and how far he remains from the ambitions of the June deal, including fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway where Iran has choked off oil and gas shipping since the fighting began.

Those inside the White House are well aware that they will blow past Monday’s deadline and that the conflict has largely morphed into one of economic warfare, according to two Americans familiar with the negotiations.

The current strategy bears a striking resemblance to previous, yearslong U.S. attempts to isolate Iran in the hopes of compelling it to abandon its nuclear ambitions. The policy had mixed results, and some analysts are skeptical that even severe economic pressure on its own will force Iran to change course. After all, that was the approach Mr. Trump attempted in his first term, even though his Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said last week that he was about to impose financial penalties unlike any seen before.

The June memorandum of understanding was widely seen as a boon for Iran, granting the regime badly needed sanctions relief even as talks over tough concessions like nuclear enrichment were postponed for later. But Iranian leaders opted to escalate again rather than consolidate their gains from the deal, according to Nate Swanson, an Iran expert at the Atlantic Council, a Washington-based research group.

Ships could move through the Strait of Hormuz freely before the war. Iran’s insistence that the deal’s vague language on the issue gave it control over the waterway led to the deal falling apart. Iran began firing on ships that transited in channels outside Iranian waters, and American forces retaliated by bombing southern Iran, prompting a cycle of attacks and counterattacks across the Middle East.

Now, Iran refuses to reopen the strait until the United States follows through on its commitments from the cease-fire, like releasing frozen Iranian assets abroad. The Trump administration wants Iran to first end the blockade, said Ali Vaez, an Iran expert at the International Crisis Group, a research institute.

“Neither side is really ready to finalize a deal. They both think that in a matter of days or weeks, the other side will be more desperate for a deal, so they’ll be able to get more out of it,” Mr. Vaez said. “This is why we are locked into this game of endurance again.”

On Saturday, the United Arab Emirates’ foreign ministry slammed Iran for attacking a vessel affiliated with the state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company the previous day. Iranian officials did not comment.

Reopening the strait has increasingly become Mr. Trump’s main focus in the conflict, even though he initially said the war was meant to empower the Iranian people to overthrow the existing regime, severely degrade its missile capability and stop Tehran from getting a nuclear weapon.

There has been little indication that Iran and the United States have extensively discussed the Iranian nuclear program since the cease-fire in June, let alone formulated a deal that could satisfy both sides.

Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, said over the weekend that Iran had yet to decide whether to resume talks with the United States. But the 60-day timeline was no longer relevant, he added, given that the June agreement was essentially defunct.

“We did not have a cease-fire that now needs to be extended,” Mr. Araghchi said. “We had an end to the war, which has now taken on a new status.”

Former U.S. officials who worked on Iran say the prospect of a new nuclear deal between the United States and Iran within 60 days was always remote, although the agreement provided for extensions. A previous, Obama-era, agreement took about two years of delicate talks to negotiate. Mr. Trump withdrew from that deal, called the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, in 2018.

The Trump administration hoped that the June agreement would, at the very least, open the Strait of Hormuz. But to get the deal over the line, they relied on vague language that lent credibility to Iran’s claim to dominate future shipping in the waterway, analysts said.

“It was a flawed document; it was hurried out when it wasn’t ready for prime time,” said Mr. Swanson, the Iran expert. “And they didn’t resolve the most important short-term issue, which was the strait.”

Instead, the United States and Iran now seem to be settling in for an indefinite struggle, neither at all-out war nor in a defined peace. Seeking to force Iran to accept U.S. terms, the Trump administration has brought back sanctions on Iranian oil and reinstated a naval blockade, both of which were temporarily canceled by the agreement.

Iran’s strained economy, which prompted mass protests that were brutally crushed early this year, is a major consideration for Iranian decision makers. But Mr. Swanson argued that the current stalemate was more likely to push Iran toward escalation than toward conciliation.

While there has been little progress on the commitments outlined in the agreement, Mr. Trump and his Iranian counterparts have continued to exchange a war of words.

During an event in Garden City, N.Y., on Friday, Mr. Trump appeared once again intent on changing the narrative, saying he would soon be “declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.”

It was not clear how serious Mr. Trump’s proposal was. But doing so could involve deploying boots on the ground and almost certainly would require a prolonged Navy presence — moves antithetical to the “America First” values of Trump supporters who want an end to prolonged military conflicts overseas.

Mr. Trump has also been known to toss out half-baked ideas on foreign policy to redirect attention and scrutiny, like when he shocked the world last year by proposing a U.S. takeover of the Gaza Strip, an idea that never materialized.

The White House on Saturday did not respond to questions over whether the administration had developed actual plans to take control of the Strait of Hormuz. Mr. Trump’s aides also did not respond to questions over the approaching Monday deadline.

Iranian officials, in turn, have defied Mr. Trump as they push their own demands — including one that they had not made before war.

“Accept reality once and for all. So far, you have suffered major strategic defeats,” Kazem Gharibabadi, the Iranian deputy foreign minister, said on social media. “The Strait of Hormuz has been Iranian, is Iranian, and will remain Iranian.”
